parental_relationship.value: None of the above - parental relationship only
parental_relationship.tooltip:
PARENTAL RELATIONSHIP ONLY

Choose this option if:

  • You were never married to your co-parent; or
  • You were never in a civil partnership with them; or
  • You have never cohabited with your co-parent.
This is the right option if:
  • The only relationship between you is having had a child or children together; or
  • Your co-parent has died and you need advice about a claim (on behalf of your children) against their estate.

Why is my relationship status important?

The law provides for various rights, protections and responsibilities (usually of a financial nature) for married couples, civil partners and cohabitees. By choosing this option you are telling us that none of those relationship types apply to you. This just means we will concentrate more upon the welfare issues for your child or children and ask different questions about financial matters.
parental_relationship.additional_description: Thank you. You have told us that the only relevant relationship status with your current or ex-partner arises through having had a child or children together.The most common type of dispute between parents is over child arrangements such as how much time the children may reside with each parent or over the split of holiday time. In some limited circumstances, there may be financial claims but only on behalf of the children. Family specialists refer to these types of financial claims on behalf of children as Schedule I claims. Just to be clear: by selecting this option you are confirming that you have never been married to your partner, in a civil partnership with them, and you have never cohabited with them in the same home. If this is correct then please proceed. If this is not correct, please change your earlier selection to one of marriage, civil partnership or cohabitation so we can ask you questions relevant to your specific circumstances.

  • Or, you are already separated or thinking of a separation from your married partner;
  • And, you need guidance on finances following your divorce or separation;
  • And/or you need guidance on child arrangements following divorce or separation;

Additionally, this choice is the right one if you are already in family court proceedings with your partner involving:

  • Matrimonial finances; or
  • Disputes over child issues; or
  • Appeals, variations or set asides of earlier court orders

pre_nuptial_agreement.value: I intend to marry my partner and need advice about a pre-nuptial agreement
pre_nuptial_agreement.tooltip:
Your relationship with your partner is strong. It will transition into one of marriage.This choice is the right one if:

  • you would like to reach an agreement with your partner before your marriage(a pre-nuptial agreement) over finances or other issues you and your partner regard as important;
  • And, you wish to provide greater certainty on the precise terms of a financial settlement in the unlikely event there is a separation or divorce in the future.

post_nuptial_agreement.value: I am married and I need advice about a post-nuptial agreement
post_nuptial_agreement.tooltip:
Your marriage with your partner is strong. This is the right choice if:

  • Your marriage is going to continue;
  • You would like to agree with your partner what happens to capital and income should there be a divorce (a post-nuptial agreement);
  • You do not have a pre-nuptial agreement prior to your marriage;
  • Or, you may have a pre-nuptial agreement prior to your marriage but feel an updated agreement (a post-nuptial agreement) is sensible.
  • And, you would like to enter into a post-nuptial agreement now while you are on good terms rather than have a fight over finances if there is a divorce in the future.

financial_claims_overseas_divorce.value: I have been divorced abroad and need advice about financial orders against my ex-partner in the English Welsh Courts
financial_claims_overseas_divorce.tooltip:
You have already been divorced in a foreign jurisdiction. This is the right choice if:

  • You and your former spouse were divorced in a foreign jurisdiction (that, is, outside of England & Wales);
  • And, that foreign jurisdiction has not been able to deal with financial assets in England & Wales.
  • And, you would like to see if the assets in England & Wales can be the subject of a financial claim;

Additionally, this choice is the right one if:

  • the court proceedings have already begun; or
  • the court proceedings have finished but there is an appeal, variation or set aside of an earlier court order.

financial_claims_on_death_of_spouse.value: My partner or ex-partner has died and I need advice about a financial claim against their estate
financial_claims_on_death_of_spouse.tooltip:
Your married (or former married) partner has died. This is the right choice if:

  • Your partner has not left a valid Will (which means the intestacy provisions apply);
  • Or, your partner has left a valid Will but the financial provision under the Will may not be that favourable to you and/or your minor children.
  • Or, it may be that someone else is claiming against your late partner's estate and you are worried about how this affects you and/or your minor children.

Additionally, this choice is the right one if:

  • relevant court proceedings have already begun; or
  • the court proceedings have finished but there is an appeal, variation or set aside of an earlier court order.

1.tooltip:
DOMESTIC ABUSE

Domestic abuse is defined by the UK Government as: any incident of controlling, coercive or threatening behaviour, violence or abuse between those aged 16 or over who are or have been intimate partners or family members, regardless of their gender or sexuality.

Coercive behaviour means an act or a pattern of acts of assault, threats, humiliation and intimidation or other abuse that is used to harm, punish, or frighten the victim.

Controlling behaviour means an act or pattern of acts designed to make a person subordinate and/or dependent by isolating them from sources of support, exploiting their resources and capacities for personal gain, depriving them of the means needed for independence, resistance and escape and regulating their everyday behaviour.

Domestic abuse occurs across all sections of society and is often under-reported to the police. Both men and women can be victims of domestic abuse. However, research suggests that around 90% of domestic abuse sufferers are women. Domestic abuse also appears more likely to occur during pregnancy, financial disputes or pressures between couples or during disputes over child arrangements.

Children suffer when they witness domestic abuse. Research has suggested that children had been in the same or adjacent room in 90% of cases when a violent assault took place.

Examples of domestic abuse and coercive control

Physical abuse

Hitting, pushing, strangling, burning with cigarettes or using weapons. Bruising may not always be present, particularly where it could be seen by others. The sufferer of such abuse may hide any marks behind clothing or sunglasses.

Emotional abuse

Threats to harm the victim, children, other family members or pets; constant criticism and humiliation of the victim; jealousy; prevention of the victim having a social or work life or contact with family. Also threats to self-harm and blame the victim, threats or actual damage to personal possessions or property belonging to the victim.

Financial abuse

Controlling money; having to justify all expenditure; not being allowed to work, or in the alternative having to hand over wages; using family funds (including benefits) for personal pleasures, such as alcohol.

Sexual abuse

Forcing sex, or withholding it, using pornography or other aids without consent, forcing to have sex with others, controlling or refusing contraception.

Resources and other help

Freephone 24 hr National Domestic Violence Helpline Run in partnership between Women's Aid & Refuge: 0808 2000 247

www.womensaid.org.uk

Offers a free 24 hour National Domestic Violence Helpline and an online guide The Survivors Handbook available as a PDF download. Children may also benefit from visiting their kids website called The Hideout. Provides a list of regional centres and services see the Domestic Abuse Directory on the home page.

MALE (Men's advice line and enquiries)

0808 801 0327

www.mensadviceline.org.uk

Support and advice for male victims of domestic violence, information for their families and for men who want to change their violent and abusive behaviour. Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday 10am - 1pm and 2pm - 5pm.

yes_do_it_yourself.tooltip: Do It Yourself The DIY option is where differences are resolved through informal discussions without any direct professional assistance. You and your partner attempt to agree things between yourselves.

yes_collaborative_model.tooltip: Collaborative Model This option involves sitting in the same room with your partner to discuss and explore solutions. But instead of having a mediator in the room, each person has their own specially trained lawyer to help in the discussions.

yes_lawyer_led_negotiation.tooltip: Lawyer-led negotiation This option involves lawyers appointed by each person; the lawyers conduct the communications by telephone, formal letters or sometimes a 'round table' meeting so the individuals and their lawyers can negotiate face-to-face.

yes_one_lawyer_one_couple_model.value: Yes, One Lawyer, One Couple Model
yes_one_lawyer_one_couple_model.tooltip: One Lawyer, One Couple This allows one lawyer, usually a neutral solicitor, to meet with and advise both parties. The advice is given to the couple in the same room so it reduces the chances of misunderstanding and conflict.

yes_financial_arbitration.tooltip: Financial Arbitration This involves an arbitrator (usually a senior lawyer) giving a legally binding decision (an ‘Award’) to resolve a range of family related financial issues.

yes_children_arbitration.tooltip: Children Arbitration This involves an arbitrator (usually a senior lawyer) giving a legally binding decision to resolve disputes over child care arrangements.

yes_early_neutral_evaluation.tooltip: Early Neutral Evaluation This process is often at the early stages of a family matter where an experienced and neutral family practitioner (often a retired judge/ barrister/experienced solicitor) will express a non-binding view upon the likely issues. This neutral person will give a balanced indication of how the dispute might be decided if it goes into a more formal process such as a family court or arbitration. This process can be used for finance and children issues and helps focus minds at an early stage to save time, money and avoid the stress of legal proceedings.

yes_private_fdr.tooltip: Private FDR FDR stands for Financial Dispute Resolution - a process usually used at the later stages of a family matter, often after formal legal proceedings have begun and often when a trial or final hearing is the next expected step. A neutral family practitioner (often a retired judge/barrister/experienced solicitor) will be asked to express a non-binding view on how the issues in dispute might be decided at trial before a court or tribunal. This process can be used for finance issues. It is used to avoid the significant expense and stress of a trial, as well as the delays caused by pressures on the court system.

yes_court_proceedings.tooltip: Court proceedings This option involves the family court where a judge will have control of the timing and the steps to be taken before a final hearing takes place.

When should I choose to just focus on children?

Family law specialists need a great deal of information in order to advise our clients properly. Very often, we can identify important issues that you may not have been aware of. However, you may want to prioritise receiving advice about immediate issues or concerns you have for your children. Just be mindful that your family specialist will find it harder to answer any wider questions about finance (including child maintenance) or property if you choose to solely focus on welfare issues for the children.

Example: Mike is going through a divorce and is now separated from his wife. Mike knows he needs advice about a financial settlement. But his immediate concern is that he is having stressful arguments with his wife about living arrangements for their children. Mike's wife appears to have stopped the children seeing Mike so he decides to prioritise getting advice about the children now. He will come back for advice about the financial settlement later. Mike can answer 'yes' to this question.

Example: Molly has separated from her husband. They run two businesses together and have three children. Molly is not sure if the family home will have to be sold and it is a problem because she runs her business from home. Whilst there is some disagreement between Molly and her husband about aspects of child care and future arrangements, it is not urgent or concerning. Molly should provide a full submission as the financial aspects of her circumstances and the interests of her children are best dealt with as a whole.

1.additional_content:
What does 'Child of the Family' mean?

A child of the family in relation to a marriage or civil partnership is defined as:

  • A child of both you and your spouse; and
  • Any other child who has been treated by both of you as a child of the family

Many families include children from previous relationships. In most cases, responsibility for caring for such children is accepted by the non-biological parent. There may be some exceptional cases where one spouse objects to a child being treated as a child of the family upon divorce or civil partnership dissolution. What if we are foster parents? Please note that a child placed temporarily with you and your spouse in your capacity as foster parents is NOT treated as a child of the family. What about 'illegitimate' children? A child born to you or to your spouse during the course of the marriage where only one of you is the biological parent is still regarded as a child of the family if treated as such by both of you. What if any children were conceived with IVF? Any child born using assisted reproductive techniques will be a child of the family.

1.tooltip:
Paying for Legal Fees

Unfortunately, most family law work does not fall within the scope of public funding (legal aid). However, some legal aid has been retained for cases involving domestic violence or for those eligible for assistance with mediation. You can look at the following link for more information:

http://www.justice.gov.uk/legal-aid-for-private-family-matters

As most people will not be eligible for legal aid it helps to think about the options that might be open to you to fund your legal assistance.

Please note that some aspects of family work are relatively easy to provide on a fixed fee basis, such as the formal divorce or dissolution process. But other aspects may be complicated and unpredictable and the cost may depend upon the attitude of your partner or the complexity of the financial assets, so a fixed fee may be more difficult to offer. But your family specialist will discuss this with you.

Different ways to pay for legal fees

Hourly rate. A firm will provide an estimate of costs for the work you request based on set hourly fee rates. It is usual in firms to have one or two people at least working on your matter with different hourly fee rates. One may be senior and provide more of a strategic direction on your matter. The junior lawyer may carry out most of the work at their lower hourly rate. Most firms will ask for costs on account before they start work. The amount will depend upon how much work is required at the very start of the case, especially if it is urgent work. A lawyer's bill will then be produced, usually on a monthly basis, as the work progresses which should be within the original estimate of costs. The original estimate of costs can be changed by agreement later on if the matter is much more complicated than initially revealed to the lawyers at the beginning or affected by external events over which you or the lawyers have no control.

An agreed fee. You pay one fee up front for the work specified. You have the advantage of knowing that no matter how complicated the matter may become, the agreed fee cannot be changed by the lawyer. The lawyer has the advantage of knowing that if they can deal with the work efficiently and manage any difficulties that may arise that they have an agreed sum up front which helps with their cash flow.

A fixed fee. Like an agreed fee, this is paid up front. Or it can be paid in a number of instalments. But, whereas an agreed fee cannot be changed by the lawyer or the client, a fixed fee can be changed if circumstances change.

Unbundling. Also sometimes referred to as a pay as you go model. This normally involves a client dealing with the whole of their legal matter themselves but occasionally asking a lawyer to help with particular parts that are more challenging. This may be instructing a lawyer just to deal with the drafting of one court document or to provide advocacy at one hearing (without becoming your official advocate on the court record for the whole of the proceedings). Typically, a client may only be seeing a lawyer for advice every couple of months over a period of a year or longer. This model has grown in popularity although there are risks for both clients and lawyers if the lawyer is not kept fully informed of all relevant developments that may have occurred when the lawyer has not been involved.

How do people afford to pay legal fees?

Well, it's not easy and we know that. Here are some ways clients have raised funds for legal fees.

  • Using existing savings or investments
  • Borrowing off family members
  • Borrowing off friends
  • Asking us to obtain funding from a specialist litigation loan provider
  • Getting unsecured commercial lending from a high street bank or finance company
  • Using credit cards
  • Asking for a voluntary lump sum payment from a partner to cover legal costs
  • Asking us to negotiate with a partner's lawyers to obtain a voluntary lump sum for fees
  • Seeing if a trades' union or professional body can help in any way
  • Asking us to apply to the court for an order that you receive maintenance from your partner which in some circumstances can include an order that you receive a contribution for your legal costs. (This last option is usually only successful if your partner has the financial means to pay and if you cannot raise any funds yourself through commercial lenders).

Your family specialist can discuss the various options you have.

1.question: We fully appreciate, {name}, that it can be daunting seeking legal advice. Are there any adjustments or allowances we can make so you get the most out of your consultation?
1.tooltip:
It is well known that increased stress can make it harder for us to process information. Additionally, it appears that around 1 in 5 of us are neurodivergent, that is, we process information whether spoken or written differently to people who are not neurodivergent. We hope that being given the time and space to collect your information and thoughts in Nova Engage has reduced some of the likely stress.

If you think we can help further at our meeting by making adjustments, please do tell us. For instance:

  • What signs would there be if you were struggling during our consultation?
  • What would make you feel more comfortable during our meeting?
  • What strategies do you have to help you manage stressful or emotional situations?
  • How comfortable are you dealing with reading large amounts of documents and financial information?
  • Would you like or need breaks during the initial meeting?
